title: The price of Trump's transactional diplomacy
gist: Drawing on 19th-century diplomatic history from the Concert of Europe to Tilsit and the Sino-Soviet split, the author argues Trump's transactional, quid-pro-quo approach to NATO is a trap: because great-power interests shift as fast as alliances, deals built on short-term interest rather than principle prove short-lived and can incubate new threats.

insights.claim: The author argues that if there are no eternal allies there are no eternal interests either, so alliances based on principles and periodic renegotiation are a more durable path than transactional quid-pro-quo deals.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: A framework for judging the durability of the current NATO bargain: interest-based deals are inherently unstable, raising alliance-continuity risk.
insights.quote: If there are no eternal allies, there are no eternal interests, either.
insights.locator: If there are no eternal allies

insights.claim: Transactional diplomacy is destructive not because transactions are bad but because great powers hold many competing interests, making it unpredictable which priority will dominate a given deal, turning alliances into ad-hoc coalitions with little permanence.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: Explains the instability mechanism, useful for pricing the reliability of any interest-driven security or trade arrangement.
insights.quote: the very interests that coalesced into seemingly intimate alliances could be superseded by other more immediately demanding priorities just a few years later
insights.locator: These ruptures attest to the treachery

insights.claim: The author warns that if allies come to see NATO's Article 5 collective-security guarantee as a subscription up for annual renewal, it may incite hubris from revisionist powers.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: Directly flags erosion of deterrence credibility as a downstream cost of transactionalism, a key risk for European security assets.
insights.quote: what if allies begin to see NATO's Article 5 collective security guarantee as being akin to a subscription up for annual renewal? That may incite hubris from revisionist powers.
insights.locator: More alarmingly, over the long term

insights.claim: Trump's art-of-the-deal approach channels Lord Palmerston's 1848 maxim that Britain had 'no eternal allies, and no perpetual enemies', but leaders are drawing the wrong lesson: what Palmerston held eternal was the pursuit of interests, and interests shift suddenly.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: Reframes a foundational realist maxim to argue interest-chasing offers no stable anchor, sharpening how to read US foreign-policy signalling.
insights.quote: What was eternal to Palmerston was the pursuit of interests; unlike principles, interests shift suddenly, sometimes drastically.
insights.locator: It seems unlikely that President Trump reads Hansard

insights.claim: The Concert of Europe of five gatekeeper powers kept the peace for decades after 1815 but died not from a grand rupture but from the slow accumulation of calculated transactions, a caution against reading Kissinger's idealised view of the system.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: Shows durable orders can erode incrementally through transactional choices rather than dramatic collapse, a pattern to watch in the current order.
insights.quote: This was not the result of a grand rupture, but the slow accumulation of calculated transactions and decisions in the ensuing decades.
insights.locator: Yet what Kissinger's idealised view overlooks

insights.claim: Austria and Russia, supposedly intimate allies after Russia crushed the 1849 Hungarian Revolution to save the Habsburg throne, ruptured when Vienna refused to back Russian Balkan expansion, and the tsar condemned Austria as an ungrateful 'free rider'.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: A historical mirror to today's 'free rider' rhetoric, warning that gratitude and interest do not bind allies once priorities diverge.
insights.quote: the tsar condemned Austria as an ungrateful 'free rider' on Russian protection

insights.claim: The author cites Napoleon's 1807 Treaty of Tilsit with Alexander I, which collapsed into invasion within five years, and the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact as evidence that Faustian bargains with rivals invariably end in disaster.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: A pattern-recognition warning: short-term deals with adversaries delay rather than avert conflict, relevant to any US-Russia or US-China detente.
insights.quote: in time, a deal with the devil will invariably end in disaster

insights.claim: Trump's transactionalism drove European defence spending higher and procurement quicker, but Europe is surreptitiously keeping the money within its own defence-industrial base and reducing its US defence spending.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: A concrete, tradeable second-order effect: US pressure may boost European defence primes at the expense of US arms exporters.
insights.quote: Europe is surreptitiously keeping the money within the continent's own defence-industrial base, reducing its US defence spending

insights.claim: The author contends Europe is transactional today for want of capacity, not character, and that a Europe with growing economies, abundant energy, integrated capital markets and lighter regulation could avoid re-negotiating Article 5 at every summit.
insights.speaker: Ziyi Wang
insights.so_what: Links European strategic autonomy directly to economic reform, energy and capital-market integration, a structural investment thesis for the continent.
insights.quote: A Europe with growing economies, abundant energy, integrated capital markets and lighter regulation could avoid re-negotiating Article 5 at every summit.
insights.locator: This does not mean that Europe erred
